name: Pope Joan
description: Pope Joan is a quintessentially English historical card game that was immensely popular in the 18th and 19th centuries. A 'Stops' game played with a specialized rotating board, it blends sequence-building with 'Lucky Card' rewards. The game centers on the 'Pope Joan' cardâ€”the Nine of Diamondsâ€”which serves as a permanent wild card. It is a game of social interaction, anticipation, and the thrill of clearing a 'Stakes' board.

history.origins: Dates back at least to the 1700s. It is named after the mythical female Pope Joan (the Nine of Diamonds), reflecting 18th-century anti-clerical humor.
timeline: 1730s: First mentioned in gaming literature as a derivation of the French game 'ComÃ¨te'.
1837: Charles Dickens famously describes a game of Pope Joan in 'The Pickwick Papers'.
1900s: Gradually declined in popularity as games like Rummy and Bridge took over the social scene.
Present: A favorite for historical reenactment groups and collectors of antique game boards.
history.cultural: In Victorian England, Pope Joan boards were often elaborate family heirlooms made of lacquered wood or papier-mÃ¢chÃ©.
history.evolution: The removal of the 8 of Diamonds was a deliberate mechanic to create a 'Stop' at the 7 of Diamonds, ensuring the 9 of Diamonds (the Pope) would always be a special card.

setup.dealing: Deal the cards evenly, plus an extra hand (the 'Stop' hand) which remains face-down.
setup.equipment: Staking board with eight compartments (Ace, King, Queen, Jack, Game, Pope, Matrimony, Intrigue); counters or chips.

rules.objective: Win chips from the board by playing specific cards and be the first to empty your hand.
rules.gameplay: Dealer stakes the board (Pope, Matrimony, Intrigue, Ace, King, Queen, Jack, Game). Fifty-one cards are dealt evenly to players plus one face-down stop hand; the last card of the stop hand is turned for trump. Eldest leads by playing a card face up (any suit, must be lowest held). Players continue the ascending sequence in that suit until a stop (King, 7 of Diamonds, or card whose successor is in the stop hand). The player who played the stop leads the next sequence with lowest card of any suit. The 9 of Diamonds (Pope) acts as any card. Compartments are won by playing the matching trump card or, for Game, by being first to empty one's hand. First out wins the Game stake and receives one counter per card from each opponent (holder of the Pope is excused).
keyRules: Remove 8 of Diamonds before play; dealer stakes the board and deals 51 cards to players plus one stop hand, last card of stop hand is trump.
Eldest leads; play must be lowest card of a suit when leading, or next higher in suit when continuing a sequence.
Kings, 7 of Diamonds, and cards whose successor is in the stop hand are stops; the player who plays a stop leads the next sequence.
9 of Diamonds (Pope) is wild. First to empty hand wins Game stake and one counter per card from each opponent; Pope holder is exempt from payment.

strategy.basic: Keep your 'Pope'! Save the 9 of Diamonds for a moment when an opponent is building a long sequence that you can't follow. By playing the Pope, you stop their momentum and get to lead a new sequence of your own. Also, pay attention to the trump suitâ€”winning the 'Matrimony' stake (King and Queen) is often more lucrative than finishing the round first.
strategy.intermediate: The 'Stop Hand' Deduction: As cards are played, you can figure out what is in the face-down 'Stop Hand'. If a 5 of Spades is led and no one plays the 6, the 6 is definitely in the Stop Hand. This makes the 5 a permanent 'Stop' for the rest of the game. Use this knowledge to safely lead 'Dead' sequences that your opponents can't interrupt.
strategy.advanced: Stuffed-Board Management: If the 'Pope' bowl hasn't been won for 5 rounds, it will be overflowing with chips. Players will bid and play much more aggressively to name Diamonds as trumps (if the variant allows bidding). In a standard game, if you hold the 9 of Diamonds and the board is 'Fat', your primary objective should be finding a way to lead Diamonds or interrupt a sequence to play itâ€”ignore the 'Game' bowl until the Pope is out.
tips: Always lead your longest suit to try and build a sequence your opponents can't follow.
Remember: 7 of Diamonds is always a Stop because the 8 is gone. It's one of the strongest tactical cards in the deck.

variations.name: Standard stakes
variations.description: Dealer places six counters in Pope, two each in Matrimony and Intrigue, one in each of Ace, King, Queen, Jack, Game.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Stake amounts only; no engine constant overrides needed for this variant.

variations.name: Agreed counter value
variations.description: Counter or chip value is agreed by the players before the game.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Counter value is agreed at table; no engine overrides required.

variations.name: Split Matrimony or Intrigue
variations.description: When King-Queen or Queen-Jack of trumps are in different hands, stakes in those compartments are sometimes divided.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Split rules are optional; no engine overrides documented for this variant.
